Art Basel Announces New Highlights To Look Forward to at 2026 Miami Beach
Art Basel Miami Beach, General Impressions, Courtesy of Art Basel

Art Basel Miami Beach is preparing to bring the international art world together for another year. The fair has announced additional details for its 2026 edition, including major gallery presentations, digital art projects, artist conversations, and public installations throughout South Florida. With 272 exhibitors from more than 40 countries and territories, the event will offer a wide-ranging look at contemporary art and the ideas shaping it.

The newly announced gallery presentations span several generations and mediums. Brazilian artist Rosana Paulino will present her first bronze sculpture, Crisálida (2025–26), with Mendes Wood DM. Other highlights include a new painting by Shara Hughes at David Kordansky Gallery and monumental bronze sculpture by Wangechi Mutu at Gladstone. A joint presentation by Ortuzar and Crèvecœur will feature paintings by Ernie Barnes, coinciding with an exhibition of his work at ICA Miami. Miami-based Spinello Projects will also make its debut in the Galleries sector, showcasing artists from the Latin American and Caribbean diaspora.

Digital art will have an expanded presence through Zero 10: Generation, the initiative’s largest edition to date. Curated by Karen Archey and Eli Scheinman, it brings together 21 exhibitors across 19 projects. The presentations explore generative art, artificial intelligence, and emerging technologies. The program also looks to the history of digital experimentation, with a presentation on early computer art in Latin America and a new collaboration with Google Arts & Culture.

The fair’s Conversations program will explore the connections between art and other cultural fields, including sports and technology. Across four days, artists, curators, and public figures will discuss topics ranging from creative practice to identity and representation.

A dedicated Art & Sports series features NBA champion Kevin Love, soccer star Crystal Dunn, and Brooklyn Nets and New York Liberty co-owner Clara Wu Tsai. The program also includes a panel with the NFL examining portraiture and legacy in professional football.

Beyond the convention center, public art and museum exhibitions will extend the experience across Greater Miami. In Collins Park, Between Tides , a collaboration with Public Art Fund, transforms six ping-pong tables into playable sculptural installations designed by artists.
The Art Basel Awards will also return for a second year, recognizing achievements across the contemporary art world. The winners will be announced at a ceremony at Miami Beach’s New World Center.
Art Basel Miami Beach takes place Dec. 4–6, at the Miami Beach Convention Center. VIP preview days are scheduled for December 2–3.

Photographer Shares the Emotional Story Behind an Elephant Carrying Its Stillborn Calf [Interview]

Wildlife photographer Federico Veronesi encountered the shot of a lifetime in Damaraland, Namibia. In September 2025, he witnessed a desert elephant carrying its stillborn calf. What resulted was an arresting black-and-white image that is beautifully composed but ultimately full of grief. The close-up portrait shows the mother with her deceased calf between her tusk and trunk, as if she is unable to let her baby go. The emotional image, titled The Aftermath , was recognized in the prestigious Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 competition , with Veronesi earning the title of Overall Winner and the Behavior Mammals category winner.

Veronesi was tracking elephants when he noticed an unusual pattern of drag marks in the sand of a dry riverbed. He understood why when he saw the mother and child. “The calf’s body rose up and in this particular frame, it almost looks like the calf is still alive, playing with its mother or trying to cling to her mother’s trunk,” he recalls to My Modern Met. “I feel that the ambiguity of the image, and how it can be read in many ways make it stand out from the other images I took, where the calf is clearly hanging lifeless from the mother’s tusk.”

The photographer initially felt conflicted about capturing the scene. “After taking the first few images, I felt like I was violating the elephant’s intimate moment, her grief, I was almost ashamed and thought that I shouldn’t take these photographs,” he shares. But ultimately, Veronesi found it important to highlight the complexity of these creatures. Elephants have been observed engaging in behaviors around death, including vocalizing, guarding the deceased, and carrying the dead, as pictured. By photographing this painful moment, Veronesi shows us that wildlife and humans aren’t as far apart as we may think.
We spoke with Veronesi about capturing the poignant shot, his philosophy about photographing wildlife, and more. Scroll down for My Modern Met’s exclusive interview.
What is your photography background, and how did you begin photographing wildlife?

Photography was part of my life since an early age as I grew up in a family of keen nature photographers. Every travel or outing was always centered on photographing nature, birds and wildlife in particular. I therefore learned photography almost naturally. I began photographing wildlife with my Polaroid on my first trip to Africa when I was 6 years old or to the local zoos and safari parks. During my teenage years I upgraded to a reflex camera and slides, and that’s what I used for my first years in Kenya after I moved there in 2002 to follow my dream of living among wildlife and photographing it full time.
Set up the scene for your image The Aftermath , which shows an elephant carrying a dead calf. How did you come across this?

I was in Damaraland, northwestern Namibia, with the specific aim to photograph desert-adapted elephants and other wildlife living in this particularly dry but stunning ecosystem. Elephants are frequently found along the dry riverbeds that traverse this landscape, as that’s where they find some trees and vegetation that they can feed on. I had seen a family of elephants the previous evening, so that morning I returned to the place where I left them to pick up their tracks and hopefully find them again. As I followed the tracks, I noticed an unusual dragging mark on the ground, which I wasn’t immediately able to interpret. Shortly after I finally came across the elephants feeding on the river banks. Out of the group, a female appeared carrying a dead calf by wedging the calf’s leg between her trunk and tusk.

Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos
In 'The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse,' the British-Turkish photographer captures a portrait of the region's living heritage.

Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia , a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse , photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak , which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.
The book is available for purchase directly from Hemeria , and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram .

Art Miami and CONTEXT Art Miami Announce 2026 Exhibitors for Miami Art Week

This December, Miami becomes the place to be for art lovers. Art Miami and its sister fair, CONTEXT Art Miami , have just revealed their participating artists and galleries for 2026, and the lineup doesn’t disappoint. Returning to One Herald Plaza, Dec. 1–6, the two fairs will bring together an international mix of galleries, artists, collectors, and contemporary art enthusiasts for the 36th edition of Art Miami and the 14th edition of CONTEXT.

Art Miami 2026 will feature work from galleries hailing from 25 countries, representing major art destinations including London, Paris, Berlin, Seoul, Hong Kong, Dubai, Istanbul, and Bogotá. Visitors can enjoy both modern and contemporary art, from the modern masters and Pop Art icons of the 20th century to contemporary painting , sculpture, photography, design, and new media.

Returning exhibitors include Allouche Gallery , Ascaso Gallery , Boccara Gallery , Ethan Cohen Gallery , and Opera Gallery , alongside more than 20 galleries from Miami and the surrounding South Florida region. Artist Lucy Sparrow will also return following the success of her felt candy store installation at last year’s fair. She will reveal her new installation, The Money Laundry , a hand-felted, interactive laundromat featuring hand-painted cash, passports, and luxury watches.

Meanwhile, CONTEXT Art Miami will once again shine a spotlight on emerging and mid-career artists. Its 14th edition will feature international galleries presenting new and recent works, solo exhibitions, curated projects, and immersive installations. Participating galleries include Bel-Air Fine Art , Hilton Contemporary , Iconic Images Gallery , and Uniquity Art Gallery , among many others.

Another major highlight across both fairs will be the celebration of artist and activist Shepard Fairey , who will receive the 2026 Art Miami Lifetime Visionary Award. Recognized for his influential practice spanning street art, graphic design, and political activism, Fairey will be honored with a curated presentation of his work in Art Miami's VIP Lounge.
Both Art Miami and CONTEXT Art Miami run between Dec. 1–6, at One Herald Plaza in Downtown Miami. Tickets are available online at Art Miami and CONTEXT Art Miami .

Andrew Hopgood is an Australian artist from Melbourne whose practice brings together illustration, oil painting and sculpture. Having started his artistic journey in illustration, he expanded into painting and sculpture around 2019, developing a visual language that combines realism with subtle surrealist elements. Much of his work centres on the natural world, particularly endangered species and the challenges wildlife faces as its environment continues to change. Through carefully constructed compositions, Andrew captures the beauty and presence of animals while drawing attention to their vulnerability and the importance of protecting the world they inhabit.

A defining feature of Andrew’s work is the way he blurs the boundaries between reality and fantasy. His compositions often place familiar elements of nature within imagined settings, creating scenes that feel at once recognizable and otherworldly.

These dreamlike environments allow him to explore the environmental pressures affecting wildlife while also considering the possibility of adaptation and survival. Rather than focusing solely on the loss and uncertainty surrounding endangered species, He introduces subtle moments of hope, imagining a natural world that continues to find ways forward. Through this balance of realism and imagination, he encourages viewers to look more closely at the relationship between humans and the environment, and to consider the role we play in shaping its future.

Joa Vilallonga is a Peruvian American contemporary artist based in Florida. She completed coursework at the Escuela Nacional de Bellas Artes in Lima before earning a BFA in Illustration, summa cum laude, from the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York. In 2017, she received FIT’s Antonio López Alumni Grant.

Her practice spans painting, sculpture, and poetry, with figurative portraiture at its core. Through layered surfaces and restrained tonal transitions, she creates a contemplative atmosphere that defines her visual language. Her paintings unfold as an exploration of stillness, perception, and emotional presence. Her work has been presented in group exhibitions in New York, Tokyo, and Tbilisi. She is a member of Unearthed, an invitation-only community for artists working in analogue, handmade media.

Joa Vilallonga’s paintings explore liminal states beyond linear time, opening visual fields where stillness becomes active. Working within contemporary figuration, she approaches portraiture as a psychological landscape. Her figures merge subtly with their surroundings, inhabiting states of silent depth. Rooted in a self-contained feminine presence, they neither seek approval nor resolution; vulnerability and strength coexist without performance.

Natural elements such as water, wind, gravity, and light function as compositional forces. Water plays a central role in her imagery, suggesting fluidity and receptivity. The human form appears permeable, shaped by transitions that soften boundaries and slow perception. Animals and small organic forms act as quiet counterparts, grounding what cannot be directly spoken.
Through restrained composition, muted palettes, and subtle luminosity, she builds contemplative images that invite sustained attention while leaving interpretation open.

A Sculptural Playground in Shanghai Is Designed for Human-Powered Play
Jump onto Wade and Leta's sculptural design in Shanghai.

In Shanghai’s Jing’an Sculpture Park, a monumental new installation by Brooklyn’s Wade and Leta has a clear goal: to get people up and moving in the same space. Titled “Catching Feelings,” the interactive artwork doubles as an all-ages playground with the artists’ signature sculptures and geometric forms. A central tower holds a quartet of slides, while other spinning and writhing elements are designed for more unstructured interaction.

“Catching Feelings” is one of 36 projects in the ninth edition of the Jing’an International Sculpture Project, an annual project helmed by the UCCA Center for Contemporary Art . In comparison to the artists’ earlier works , the bold, kinetic playground is decidedly analog, with any movement powered by the people interacting with its components rather than embedded motors or motion generated by the wind.

“We’re interested in the life and activity around our work—the behaviors it causes, the elations it brings,” the artists say in a statement. “We watched the same grandfather return with his granddaughter to play hide and seek; an 84-year-old and his partner used the space as the backdrop for their video recordings; new friends were made on our ground spinners; we even glimpsed a man in a business suit having a go on the slide.”

“Catching Feelings” is presented alongside monumental works by Olafur Eliasson , Marshmallow Laser Feast , and many others on view through December 31. Find more from Wade and Leta on their Instagram .

The New York-based artist combines delicate pencil drawings with the nostalgic graphics of the early internet, exploring intimacy and the blurry line between what’s real and what’s artificial.

A swallow perches on a white plastic garden chair beside a column of blue folder icons, apparently waiting for a download to finish. A pale sky lifted from a computer desktop frames a bird circled in red under the instruction “Enter the following”, and the answer typed in the box below reads “birds :-)”. In her artworks, Gigi Borgese draws every detail by hand, and the gentle humour really rises to the surface once you know where it all comes from.

Growing up in San Jose, California, Gigi describes herself as largely self-taught, having spent much of her life as what she calls “a passive creative”. Between the ages of 14 and 17, she was an influencer on early TikTok, where the objectification she endured and “the feelings of emptiness/futility in that content” pushed her to delete her accounts and commit to art.

She spent a year at West Valley Community College, then moved to New York in 2023 at 19. She now studies for a BFA in Studio Art at the City College of New York, with a minor in Classics, and has won the Adelaide Jablonsky Award (2025) and the Connor Merritt Award (2026). She was also a finalist in the 2026 Astor Place student art competition, and alongside her degree, she works at the Morris Jumel Mansion on public programming, prop recreation and research.

Her subject matter took shape in 2025, when she was 20. Unknown numbers began texting her doctored and AI-generated images of herself, often depicting her as a minor. “I quickly discovered an active Discord group of over 100 men who had been doing this to me for, at the time, five years,” she says. It sent her back to her years as an influencer and to larger questions around human connection online. “I would not wish that on anyone; however, I credit this event for forcing me to figure out what I wanted to say with my art.”

What she wanted to say arrives through birds, apples and flowers, forms she associates with fragility and femininity, which she then “bastardises” with the visual language of the internet. At 18, she saw Sonya Rapoport’s exhibition Force fields at the Minnesota Street Project in San Francisco, and the artist’s continuous-feed computer paper and early ASCII art “resonated with a part of me that had not yet processed the impact that the internet had on me.”

She’s also drawn to Plato’s ideas about reality and representation. “If the physical world is a flawed copy of our internal world, then the internet is a further copied and flawed version of the physical world.” That chain of copies becomes literal in her work, where you see a swallow multiplying into fading outlines, as if copied and pasted; and a pixelated bird hovering over two ordinary swallows on a yellow grid; and a row of halved green apples placed with the caption “Forbidden (What does it feel like?)”.

To build these scenes, she browses dead websites and old web interfaces, then looks at 19th-century scientific illustrations of flowers and birds. “I find similarity in this artificial attempt to capture the essence of something true,” she says. She works like one of those illustrators, “crudely recreating something with influences from digital spaces”, a method that deliberately mirrors the way the men copied her.

Beautiful Bastard (2026), the piece she says she's proudest of, started when she felt stuck in her older work. Alley-Oop, the French-born artist’s first permanent public artwork, pays tribute to a basketball legend and an architectural landmark.

If you’ve spent any time in East London, you’ll probably have come across Camille Walala’s work, albeit perhaps unknowingly; from the Dream Come True Building on Old Street to the stretch of Leyton High Street she covered in grids, triangles and stripes.

Now the French-born, London-based artist is bringing her colourful, Memphis-influenced style to the platforms of Flachet–Alain Gilles metro station in Villeurbanne, part of greater Lyon, France, which serves around 5.7 million passengers a year.

Set for completion next Spring, the installation, titled Alley-Oop, has been created from more than 30,000 hand-crafted ceramic tiles. This will be the biggest project of Camille’s career to date. It’s also her first permanent public-realm work, her first major project in her home country and her first large-scale use of ceramic tile as a material.

BrandOpus has refreshed the much-loved lager brand with a football-style crest celebrating its Burton brewing heritage and its mission of “bringing mates together”.

In the last decade or so, it feels like every British brand has tried to link itself with British football. But some have been in the game, so to speak, longer than others. And if you’re looking for authentic ties, you’ll struggle to find a better example than Carling.

For decades now, it’s been in the hands of fans on matchday, and despite the inexorable rise of hipster craft beers, this honest, reliable, easy-drinking, thirst-quenching amber nectar of a drink (can you tell it’s my favourite tipple?) still gets great love from the football crowd today.

That love has long been two-way. Carling’s name has been on cup competitions, club hoardings and more than a few pub chalkboards for as long as I can remember. And in 2026, they’re leaning into that more than ever, with a refreshed identity built around a football-style badge.

Now rolling out now across supermarkets, convenience stores, pubs and bars, the new identity, crafted by BrandOpus, aims to reimagine Carling’s role in modern culture through the language of community, quality and heritage.

At the heart of the refresh is the new badge, which evokes a sense of the crests stitched onto football shirts. The aim was to make drinking Carling feel more like being part of a team. As Paul Taylor, CCO and co-founder at BrandOpus, explains: “The creative strategy was built around Carling’s core brand purpose of bringing mates together, with all design elements crafted to convey moments of connection.

“Long used in football and communities as a symbol of shared identity, pride and connection, the badge is deployed as a visual metaphor for belonging. It reconnects Carling with its roots, while tying it back to the world of football. It makes the brand feel like a club that people are a part of.”
One good way to convey community and belonging visually is through symbols of heritage and history, and the new design is packed with those.

Inside the badge are illustrations of the historic Carling Brewery and the Burton Bridge, framed by sprigs of barley, with “The Carling Brewery” and “Burton-upon-Trent” threaded around the edge, and Carling’s Black Label banner running across the middle.
For good measure, BrandOpus also added the signature of founder and original brewer Thomas Carling to the can and the glass.

The new pint glass builds on the existing design, which BrandOpus previously helped craft as part of their long-running partnership. This version dials up the heritage messaging with the new badge, along with embossed Burton-upon-Trent lettering near the base.

BrandOpus has also developed a wider, flexible brand world that builds on Carling’s long relationship with football, from grassroots clubs to the Emirates FA Cup and the Women’s FA Cup. This includes a set of illustrated murals and out-of-home assets for stadiums and club sites, designed to adapt to each club’s colours and personality.

All this seems like a smart move for a brand that’s been around for a long time and risks being taken for granted. After all, people’s attitudes to both beer and football have changed dramatically over the past decade, and it feels like the sands are constantly shifting: incoming Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s focus on relaxing the drinking laws at football grounds stands testament to that.
Carling needed to respond to both shifts, reasserting its place in a crowded market while strengthening its ties with the game and the communities around it.

As Ryan McLaughlin, brand director for Carling at Molson Coors, puts it: “This is much more than a packaging refresh. As consumer expectations continue to evolve, it’s important that iconic brands evolve too.

“This is the latest step in Carling’s evolution, building on the strengths that have made it the leading core lager brand in Great Britain, while creating a bolder, more contemporary identity for the future.”

A new site design and wordmark for Hyperallergic’s next era.

From the start in 2009, Hyperallergic has been kicking at the doors of the art world status quo, challenging assumptions about what is worthy of investigation and investment, and the supposed neutrality of those decisions. Today, 17 years later, we are no longer a young upstart blogazine but a daily source of trusted news, reviews, and opinions for millions in the art community.

We’ve transformed our strategy for sustainable revenue and evolved our editorial approach several times over the years to meet the unique challenges of each internet era. While so many of our peers have disappeared, we’ve survived as an independent media company throughout it all. It’s never been easy, but it’s always been worth it.

As we enter yet another new era, with social media becoming ever more toxic and AI seemingly overtaking every aspect of our lives, we want to refocus ourselves on being the best place for our community to gather. For all of us to learn, to grow, to laugh, and to feel connected to each other.
Today, we are excited to introduce the next transformation of this site, with a whole new look, a dynamic homepage, and the third version of our wordmark.

It’s clear that the insistent and demanding bright cyan of the site is no longer needed, and it is time for Hyperallergic to look more like the authoritative publication it has now become. (And for those who always loved the blue, you’ll see it re-emerge in spots over time.)

The Brooklyn-based design cooperative, Partner & Partners , has created a warm and inviting new look and organizational framework that fits our evolving output and will help us expand into the future.

Our new wordmark is drawn from Hyperallergic TwoOneFive, a new custom typeface made for us by Commercial Type . It is a grotesque that harkens back to the days of the Bauhaus and is full of unique quirks that push it into the future. Letting go of the uppercase blue condensed wordmark, the new logotype leans towards classic while remaining full of energy. The high bar of the capital H leads us into the lowercase title; this itself is a marker that we no longer need the screech of all caps.

Hyperallergic is by and for art-focused readers and writers, so the site has to encourage both. Spectator, a new serif typeface also from Commercial Type, brings a richness and warmth to the screen. Compared with more traditional typefaces, Spectator is clean with soft corners and is bolder all around, encouraging the eye to move from line to line.
We’re foregrounding our authors' names to highlight our team and many guest contributors, and the effort and care that goes into all the work you see on the site.

With a vast archive of tens of thousands of posts from thousands of writers and spanning nearly two decades, we’ve built a whole new search experience and a reorganized tagging system to allow readers to discover connections between writers, themes, and subjects that might otherwise get lost.
This new site design allows for more diversity in article layouts and lets us give prominence on our homepage to stories we think deserve more of your attention.

But ultimately, one of the design’s strongest elements is its ability to get out of the way. While vastly improving the user experience, it rarely draws attention to itself, instead allowing the focus to be on the content of the site, rather than the frame.

This redesign is just one part of a bigger shift. You may have noticed we now ask you to sign in to a free account to read most articles. That’s because we want to build a closer relationship with our readers and a more sustainable platform to publish the news, reviews, and commentary that keep you engaged, informed, inspired, and entertained. All while speaking truth and challenging the status quo in the art world.

Open-source tools like Ghost allow us to remain insulated from the whims of platforms funded by venture capital, with sky-high investments and unrealistic valuations that inevitably force them to pivot or shut down. Tools like these have allowed us to keep publishing without fear for the past 17 years and invest in what matters most: connecting our writers to our readers.

British street artist Helen Bur has completed her largest mural to date in Bordeaux, France, transforming the towering façade of the Nerval residential building in the Grand Parc neighbourhood into a monumental portrait of motherhood, female solidarity and human connection. Entitled Matrescense , the artwork depicts two local women in the final trimester of pregnancy, brought together through a project that celebrates the importance of companionship and mutual support within the community.
Helen Bur, WIP, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The title, Matrescence , refers to the profound transition into motherhood, a developmental process encompassing the physical, psychological, emotional and social changes experienced as a woman becomes a mother. Much like adolescence, it is a period of transformation in which identity, relationships and perceptions of self evolve.

Through her portrayal of two expectant mothers, Helen Bur gives this often overlooked experience a monumental public presence, recognising not only the vulnerability and anticipation of pregnancy but also the importance of connection, understanding and mutual support during one of life’s most significant transitions.
Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Created for KIFKIF, an ambitious urban art initiative led by Bordeaux-based association EXIT, the mural marks the beginning of a wider programme connecting internationally recognised artists with local residents through public art, creative workshops and community participation.

At the heart of Matrescense are two pregnant women arranged head-to-foot, their bodies forming an intimate, almost circular composition reminiscent of the yin-yang symbol. One reclines towards the ground while the other turns upwards, their opposing positions creating a sense of balance and interdependence. Although each woman occupies her own space within the painting, their gestures and proximity suggest an unspoken relationship built upon understanding, companionship and mutual care.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Both women live in Bordeaux’s Grand Parc neighbourhood and were invited to become models for the artwork. Remarkably, they had not known one another before the project, making their connection something that developed through the creative process itself. What appears to be a longstanding bond between two women was, in fact, formed through the experience of participating in the mural.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The subject emerged from Helen Bur’s exploration of the neighbourhood’s social realities, particularly the experiences of women raising children without a partner. Rather than portraying motherhood through an idealised image of the family, she places two expectant mothers together, acknowledging the friendships, relationships and wider networks of support that can become essential throughout pregnancy and parenthood.
Matrescense: Intimacy on a Monumental Scale

Rising across the façade of the Nerval building, the 32-metre mural transforms an ordinary residential elevation into an expansive, deeply personal painting. Completed following more than two weeks on site, despite challenging weather conditions, the work represents a significant milestone in Bur’s artistic practice.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The composition is particularly striking for the contrast between its monumental scale and the intimacy of its subject. The two women appear suspended within a richly layered interior of deep terracotta, warm ochre and patterned textiles, surrounded by abundant green foliage. The arrangement creates the impression of a private domestic space opened to the city, allowing an everyday moment of connection to occupy the architecture of an entire building.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The term “ J-Horror ” seems pretty straightforward, but as it turns out, it doesn’t just mean “ Japanese horror ” . Or rather, it’s not a catch-all for every offering of Japanese horror—it better describes a particular movement and style. However, regardless of where you land on this topic, there is no argument that Kiyoshi Kurosawa is a key figure in J-Horror.

Well before making waves with Pulse (2001), Kurosawa had already established himself in Japanese horror. These productions, all of which predate his career benchmark Cure (1997), go overlooked by the masses , but it’s his film Door III (1996) that helped shape what we now know as Kurosawa’s signature style.

After dabbling with the pink film genre in the early to mid-1980s— Kandagawa Pervert Wars (1983) and the pinkish Bumpkin Soup (1985)—Kurosawa embarked on his steadiest stint of horror . That first effort was 1989’s Sweet Home , a creative twist on the classic haunted house film that, for reasons, has essentially been disowned by Kurosawa . Between then and 1992’s The Guard from Underground , a Japanese slasher that commented on corporate culture, was Kurosawa’s contribution to the three-part anthology film Dangerous Stories (1989).

Shortly before breaking through with Cure , Kurosawa , along with writer Chiaki Konaka ( Serial Experiments Lain ) , delivered the third and final entry in the Door film series. Banmei Takahashi , who Kurosawa had indirectly collaborated with on Dangerous Stories , helmed the first and middle installments. Yet unlike both of its unrelated predecessors, the second sequel has a supernatural quality.

This film centers on a woman, really one of many, who has been taken against her will. Indeed, the subject matter here is hardly unheard of when visiting the sleazier side of Japanese cinema, but Door III goes about it in a different, not to mention startling, way. How the antagonist subdues and attacks his victim is as unique as it is frightening.

Being self-contained, Door III doesn’t require any knowledge of the prior two films. That said, they are recommended viewing for different reasons; Door (1988) is a suspenseful standoff between a homemaker and a deranged salesman, and Door 2: Tokyo Diary (1992) is an artful character study of a sex worker. The latter was ultimately made an in-name-only sequel, due to the success of Takahashi’s first film. Even so, there is a bit more in common between them than the fact that every story is fronted by a woman .

Door , having come out in the late Eighties, was reflecting then-modern Japan. The economic bubble was about to burst, and Banmei Takahashi captured one affected woman’s growing panic toward it. The financial strain she ( Keiko Takahashi ) and her middle-class family would soon feel, plus the loss of status, was a concern even before Daijirō Tsutsumi ’s character came knocking—later chainsawing—at her various physical doors. As for Door II , the titular object is now something intangible, yet it’s no less important to Chikako Aoyama ’s directionless Ai. She is, in a matter of speaking, going through a series of doors to find herself.

As with the first sequel, Door III is set in post-economic bubble Japan—a.k.a. the Lost Decade. You get a sense of that struggle as the main character here, ambitious insurance agent Sasaki ( Minako Tanaka ), is suddenly failing to meet her quota at work. Whatever doors in life had been opened for her, they are now closing. Yet unlike her rival, Reiko ( Rinko Mayumi ), Sasaki doesn’t resort to sleeping with customers to get sales. Soon enough, though, more tugs at the protagonist than job stress ; a potential client named Mitsuru ( Akihiro Nakazawa ) has a strange hold over Sasaki. With every following confrontation, she becomes less and less able to stop him.

Door III is akin to someone finally meeting their match. Occupationally speaking, Sasaki was well used to getting her way, and she did so with a mix of natural charm and good salesmanship. Her usual spell on clients, in this instance the mysterious Mitsuru, now doesn’t work at all, and she’s put on the receiving end of a person who won’t take “ no ” for an answer. What should a festival line-up look like in 2026?
It can be a roll of the dice as to whether a line-up is to your taste or not. Emma Wilkes investigates the changing tides of festival line-ups, from the mainstream to the obscure.

The nights are long, the year is ending, and the once-yellowing grass is now carpeted with frost, but next summer is already taking shape. Every day, it seems, there’s another fresh festival line-up threatening to knock some digits off your bank balance. I should know – I spend this time of year writing news stories about them.

If you’re a regular festival goer, or even if there’s just one particular event you count down the days to return to, it’s a time of year that can bring bated breath and crossed fingers. It can be a roll of the dice as to whether a line-up is to your taste or not. Just like music itself, it’s subjective, and there can be a difference between a festival line-up that’s not to your taste and a line-up that’s an all-round failed throw.

In the last week, I’ve seen the internet split down the middle over two line-ups in particular. This year’s Manchester edition of Outbreak Festival was the most diverse yet controversial in its 15-year history, featuring “The Hayley Williams Show” headlining for two nights on the bounce and a line-up co-curated by Hayley Williams itself, with fewer traditional hardcore acts and wider-spanning alternative names including Wednesday, American Football and Julien Baker. Some were instantly hooked, others – especially Outbreak’s more traditional fans – feeling like the festival had changed beyond recognition.

A couple of days later, Glastonbury unveiled its line-up poster some months earlier than expected. It had the youngest headliners this side of the millennium, in the form of 33-year-old Sam Fender and Harry Styles and 25-year-old returning headliner Billie Eilish, while the rest of the bill leaned younger and more pop-heavy. The Instagram comments paint a divided picture, especially among older Glasto-goers feeling pushed out, or guitar fans feeling it was all a little anaemic with a limited offering for their tastes.

Neither of these are ‘bad’ bills, per se. The Outbreak line-up I love, and the Glasto line-up I appreciate but am relatively unmoved by. But viewed through a lens of objectivity rather than subjectivity, what makes a ‘good’ festival bill?

The crucial question is what a festival is for. Sure, it’s a weekend to dance with your friends, explore music, tick off bucket list bands and fill your head with memories, but every festival poster is a statement. What matters in music right now? Who do people want to see? It should hold up a mirror to what culture looks like, which obviously has commercial purposes as a means to promote an album, but there’s an element of artistic value to it too.

The relevant question to ask could be ‘Is it current?’, but not all festivals necessarily operate with that energy, so perhaps the better one is, ‘Is it relevant?’ Are you booking bands that feel of the moment, whether they’re breaking out or surging back into fashion, or milking the nostalgia cash cow?

Equally important is variety. What’s the use of booking the same bands that do the rounds every year, or the same sort of sounds? There’s an element of curation involved. What sort of vibe is the day going to have? How much choice is there of who to see at a particular time? And it goes without saying - if it’s mostly male and pale from top to bottom, it loses relevancy points. There’s something deeply retrograde about not taking heed of the genuinely meaningful calls for more people to see artists who look like them on festival stages.

There’s also an aspect of cultural responsibility too. The smaller stages of a festival can offer formative experiences for the heroes of the future to draw new fans in and develop how they perform. Festivals need to make the space to nurture that talent, especially those coming up through the grassroots. It’s why it felt like such a disappointment to see Reading and Leeds cut the BBC Introducing stage, and pad out its replacement stage, The Canopy, with nepo babies who may not need the boost. By contrast, the Cheltenham-based 2000trees has always been brilliant at building up new bands, booking them year after year, and creating a culture of what’s known as ‘Trees bands’ who the fans love just as much as they love the festival.

In 2004, The Scream was stolen. It was finally recovered after the reward became 2,000,000 M&Ms
On January 22nd, 1892, Edvard Munch had a panic attack.

The esteemed artist was walking with two friends along a fjord in Oslo, Norway, before he took a moment to collect himself on the fence running between the shore and the water. He would later say that in that moment, “I sensed an infinite scream passing through nature.”

That’s a feeling that would shake anyone to their core. However, Munch at least had a way of expressing it. He turned that image into a sort of self-portrait. Putting a proxy of himself at the very centre of it, except rather than just feeling the torment within, this new version was actively vocalising what Munch felt was passing through nature. Under a blood-red and pus-yellow sky, and a river stretching out of whirling blues and whites, the subject of the painting turns to face the viewer, hands clasping their face as they let out The Scream .

It’s one of the more bizarre works of art to become as globally, undeniably famous as it is. It’s by no stretch of the imagination beautiful the way that something like Mona Lisa , Sunflowers or Girl With a Pearl Earring is. This isn’t something that makes any viewer feel good or “enriched” in the traditional sense. In fact, quite the opposite.

It’s no surprise to find that the inspiration for the work was a literal panic attack; one can feel that ineffable feeling of dread and hopelessness at its core. Yet it’s also one of the most valuable works of art ever created.

Which is truly baffling. Not because it’s not a staggering artistic achievement, but since when has the market for high art ever rewarded things for being staggering artistic achievements? It’s like if Joy Division’s ‘Atmosphere’ became one of the biggest-selling singles of all time. It’s not like it doesn’t deserve it, or that everyone hasn’t been in that kind of a dark place before, but still, works of art depicting those mental states don’t often get so ubiquitous.

In that case, perhaps its fitting that the moment The Scream became the target of one of the most infamous art heists of all time, it wasn’t in some Thomas Crown Affair style daring, style heist, but something that more resembled a mugging.

In 2004, The Scream had long been removed from the commercial sales market and was owned by the City of Oslo. It was the crown jewel of the city’s Munch Museum, and on the morning of Sunday, August 22nd, two masked men with guns burst into the gallery, making a beeline for the iconic painting.

While one of them held gallery staff and tourists alike at gunpoint, forcing them onto the floor, the other set about ripping The Scream and another Munch masterwork, titled Madonna , off the wall with his bare hands. These were clearly not criminal masterminds, as they literally dropped Madonna on the floor as they ran for the exit, but the gambit worked and two years later, the painting still remained at large.
Oslo had offered a two million kroner reward for any information that led to the painting’s recovery, but in 2006, it seemed that the deal had to be quite literally sweetened.

M&Ms were launching a new dark chocolate flavour, and for some bizarre reason, the company thought to offer a reward alongside Oslo’s financial reward. They said that whoever helped recover the painting wouldn’t just receive two million kroner, they’d also receive two million M&Ms. This put some serious egg on their face when the painting was uncovered thanks to a tip-off from a convicted criminal who revealed the painting’s location as a way of securing a lighter sentence.

Not wanting to give a metric ton of candy to a literal criminal, M&Ms changed course slightly and instead gave the monetary value of two million pieces of their candy (around 140,000 kroner) to the Munch Museum to help with its restoration.

The cruel world of Octopus Wrestling, the most bizarre sport ever which was finally banned in 1976
People really will watch anything, won't they?
One wonders what the editors of Mechanix Illustrated magazine thought when they received a pitch for an article about the writer’s sport of choice, titled ‘Octopus Wrestling is my Hobby’.

In fairness, perhaps it was because the year was 1949. Anything that could keep people’s minds off that thing that ended four years ago was worth a try. Especially considering the emergence of all the horrifying secrets the enemy was keeping. The war was over only in terms of he cessation of conflict, but the world kept going in its shadow for decades. So God help us all, sometimes we just need to stop thinking about the world and start thinking about some freak who wrestles sea creatures for his kicks.

The author wasn’t kidding either. Wilmon Menard wrote about his time in Tahiti, where he assisted local hunters in taking to the water and killing an octopus that Menard said had 25-foot-long tentacles. The absorbing way he wrote about this experience, plus his insistence that it had done amazing things for his mental and physical health, meant that the article became a sensation. So much so that diving clubs in the Pacific Northwest thought this would be a brilliant idea to adapt into a proper sport.

The first thing they did was remove the killing of it all. This wouldn’t be competitive hunting because that would be barbaric , especially considering the quarry and its rarity in parts of the ocean accessible to humans. The first version of this article adapted into a proper sport came from the Puget Mud Sharks Diving Club, where they would mark out an area between 30 and 60 feet into the sea. Then one team would dive down, coax out one of the octopuses just going about its day, then capture it and take it to land.

There, the octopus would be weighed and then released. The divers would then be given points based on the weight of their quarry, which would be doubled if they brought it to the surface without scuba gear. Other diving clubs took this rule set and began using it themselves, and suddenly, clubs would compete in octopus wrestling competitions that would attract crowds of hundreds. If you think people would just watch anything pre-TV out of boredom, you’re actually not quite right.

Perhaps it was morbid curiosity, but people tuned in to keep track of the octopus wrestling in droves. Not only as a flash-in-the-pan novelty either, but in the 1960s, there were World Octopus Wrestling Championships that attracted crowds of thousands in person and hundreds of thousands on TV. People clowned on Marty Mauser in Marty Supreme for his belief that the next big sport was ping-pong, but considering that octopus wrestling was gaining momentum at the time that film was set, maybe he had a point.

However, it couldn’t last for two reasons. For one thing, octopus wrestling was incredibly exciting… if you were 50 feet under the water where it was actually happening. Crowds in person weren’t, and TV technology of the 1960s couldn’t possibly put a camera down there. So normal people got bored of the spectacle real quick. Then the 1970s came, and the other shoe dropped. You see, by that time, the tech had been made to just about film professionally underwater, and Jacques Cousteau had used it to make Octopus, Octopus , a still astonishing documentary about how smart, gentle and all-around amazing our eight-tentacled friends are.

It was a massive hit, and suddenly, octopus wrestling began to be seen as cruel even if the quarry stayed alive after reaching the surface. Which, considering the struggle and the time out of the water, many of them did not. By 1976, the practice was banned, and while some people still try and match the glory days but doing illegal octopus wrestling bouts, they’re shamed on social media at best and arrested at worst.
Just as it should be, to be fair.

What do 35 years of touring the UK look like to Manic Street Preachers?
Here’s what Nicky Wire remembers best, as told to The Quietus editor John Doran. An excerpt from issue one of SHOWNOTES.

I am very much a homebird, so when it came time for Manic Street Preachers to go on tour I was nervous about it. My Dad had an old grandad’s chair, which he managed to tie to the wall in the back of the hire van, so someone could have a seat on the way to the gig. It was incredibly dangerous. And then on the way back, James would just get in a sleeping bag and lie down in the back of the van, rolling around all over the place as we were driving back home. He can sleep anywhere.

We had such a deep bonding experience on the Motown Junk Tour in 1991. The staff at the venues were just so friendly; you felt that they really cared. I remember getting to the Stoke Wheatsheaf – a magical venue – and we hadn’t had any food for a day and a half. They made us the most beautiful burger and chips.

King Tut’s Wah Wah Hut, Glasgow? The Stoker, Coventry? The Barrel Organ, Birmingham? JB’s, Dudley? Moles, Bath? The Adelphi, Hull? The Leadmill, Sheffield? It was a truly magical tour, I can’t even remember any bad shows.

The greatest one was probably The Buzz Club in Aldershot. What a fucking venue. Who’d have thought if you were in a rock band, going to Aldershot would give you one of the greatest gigs of your life? It was full of squaddies because it’s an army town, and it was antagonistic, but also brilliant. That was on the edge but some gigs could tip over the edge.

We did quite a scary gig at Reading’s After Dark Club. There was a proper firm of football hooligans there. That film The Firm had just been on TV and I don’t know if it had got people excited but it kicked off. James got punched but we stood our ground. There was a real adrenaline rush to it, even if there was a hint of violence at a lot of those early gigs.

What strikes me now is that all of these places were towns and I wonder how many of them have that kind of gig venue left. You can still play gigs in the cities, but to play in these towns was amazing: learning your trade and meeting people. Also realising there are people like you in every town you go to.

Very early doors, Little Chefs were different – they deserve an honourable mention because you could just get a proper meal there. A plate of bacon, egg and chips. We loved going to them but even by the time we started touring they were getting harder to find. And in the services before they improved, all you could find was some dodgy pasty that had been sitting in a fridge for weeks. But I have a theory that bad food equals great music. Show me a band that’s eaten healthy food all of their lives and their music is always shit. Whereas The Fall, those bands in Seattle that just lived on hard drugs and strong coffee, Sex Pistols… they lived on bad motorway service station diets and they made the greatest music. I think if you care that much about your bodily health, you’re shutting off a pathway to creativity.

Hamburg’s Seasurfer Revisits First Love in Video for “Hush Now” — “Trip” EP Out Now!
Here we are again You look so familiar In this red light… Drop your mask, my friend Someone you loved at seventeen can say your name across a room and… The post Hamburg’s Seasurfer Revisits…

Someone you loved at seventeen can say your name across a room and bring back every little thing you did to look at ease. You remember where you put your hands and the joke you made while you worked up the nerve to ask them to stay. The relief came when they heard the question in the joke and stayed a little longer. It can take years to realize how much you miss being known that well.

At the opening of “Hush Now (The Calling),” Apolonia sings to a familiar face bathed in red light, as king them to drop the mask with the gentle insistence of an old friend inviting you to sit and stay awhile. The track is the lead single from Trip , the four-track EP released November 20 by Hamburg noise-pop trio Seasurfer .

Christian Klepp ’s footage casts the first verse’s red light across the stage. Red and yellow projections sweep the back wall, while green glints in the dark glasses above a ribbed microphone. Maysterwerke cuts from this intimate close-up to wider shots, where amber haze reduces the band to little more than silhouettes.
Watch the video for Hush Now (The Calling) below.

The way the band moves in and out of view has a counterpart in the arrangements Dirk Knight began imagining in New York. “For me, this is the sound of cities,” says the instrumentalist, who recorded, produced and mixed the EP. He keeps the bass and drums fairly still while the guitars and the voices of Apolonia and Kiora drift in and out of focus.

Those guitars have been a constant since Seasurfer’s first two albums on Saint Marie Records and through collaborations with Cocteau Twins’ Robin Guthrie and producer John Fryer. This year the band put them to work on the post-punk of June’s Angels , then let them fill the room on August’s shoegaze-heavy The Noise is ours . On their third EP of 2026, a trip-hop beat gives the guitar chords more room to ring.

You can hear that space in the first bars of the opening track , One . The guitars drone and the drums take their time, leaving room for the strings that Chandeen’s Harald Löwy adds to the arrangement. The higher voices blur into the chords the way they do on My Bloody Valentine’s Loveless . The low lead comes through with the intimacy of someone speaking in confidence. It’s a seductive way to sing about making peace with your own company and the knowledge that we come and go alone.
Watch the video for One, filmed by Ahmed Sarowar and edited by Dirk Knight, below:

That intimacy carries into Hush Now (The Calling) , where a sigh of synths stretches into long, luminous lines and Knight’s guitars bring warmth up from below. Apolonia and Kiora’s voices cascade through the chorus, opening the melody out the way Elizabeth Fraser could on Cocteau Twins’ Heaven or Las Vegas and Milk & Kisses . Apolonia describes the song as a memory of first love, and Kiora hears loss and longing in the words. When the refrain comes round to “I’m by your side,” the reassurance sounds as necessary to the person giving it as it does to the one hearing it.

The guitar comes further forward on “Disappear” , where the opening loop has the woozy repetition of Cocteau Twins’ Otherness EP. The voice has Cranes’ reserve and some of Portishead’s unease. When the drums drop away, the guitar keeps circling long enough for you to stop anticipating the next hit. By the time it comes, the loop has built up a charge that carries into the closing bars.

The drums make you wait for them again on “I See You” . The guitars pile up first, with the soft-edged distortion of Loveless , and the drum machine gives them a trip-hop lilt when it comes in. There’s some of Cranes’ distance in the singing and some of the poise of Siobhan de Maré on Mono’s “Life in Mono.” At under three minutes, the closer rewards a second pass. Follow a guitar you barely noticed the first time through, and you can hear the arrangement shift around it.

Last night marked the end of my birthday week, because spending last week in Paris wasn’t enough- I had to extend it. What a gig to wrap it up with! I’ve been waiting to see C.O.F.F.I.N for what has felt like a lifetime, and last night- I finally got to see them. What made it even more special was having Gold Cup as the support.

I’ve seen Gold Cup live this year about 4 times now, and they just keep getting better and better. Despite a few technical issues at the start, they played their set as if they were the headliners. And to be honest, it won’t be long until they are headlining the Pink Room at YES. Some bands are made to be heard live, and Gold Cup are one of those bands. There’s something about their live shows that just makes you feel good and glad to be alive, y’know? I can’t wait for their debut record to come out because it’s just going to make their shows even more wild. They’re the best at what they do, and it felt like the crowd were an even split of Gold Cup and C.O.F.F.I.N fans, and you cannot help but be proud of that. The energy they have on stage and the way they play together is a thing of beauty- and yes, you will leave feeling like you want to start a band because of them.

C.O.F.F.I.N time! Where on earth do I begin? Opening the set with Out In Oslo caused the room to erupt and it pretty much stayed like that for the whole time. Part of me was watching the band, the other part was just obsessed with the crowd. It is so easy to feel unsafe at shows especially when it’s rowdy, but this felt safe. It felt like a community. And as a visibly queer person, that feeling is rare to find right now given how shit the world is. But when you find that safety net, you hold onto it. I love everything that C.O.F.F.I.N stand for, and whilst the night was ridiculously fun- they used their platform to highlight the domestic violence rates in Australia, how corrupt governments are, calling people out on their shitty behaviours and not make life harder for those of us in marginalised communities. Life is tough enough already- just be kind to each other. It’s not hard.

Every song is yelled back at the band, and there are countless stage dives and crowd surfs. You could feel the love for the band in the room, truly. And the sense of being free and being able to express yourself however you want is also felt, and that’s something we should never take for granted. You can tell that the band not only love the bones of each other but they absolutely love playing shows, and you could feel how much it meant to them. I spent the time in awe of Ben because anyone who can sing AND drum at the same time is someone to admire (within reason because there are some people who can do it but y’know…)

Every song is greeted with people in the front throwing their sweaty bodies into each other and having the time of their lives. Some of them may be feeling it today but who cares! The joy on their faces, arms around their mates and strangers- it was so lovely to see because the world is unkind, but that energy did not step foot into the room once last night. What C.O.F.F.I.N have created with their music and live shows is a safe space, and that’s something to really hold onto. For me songs like Fast Love (this was my favourite and it was a tough call) and Give Me A Bite were WILD! Think Bad absolutely ripped too as did White Dog.

You really, really felt the love for the band when they left and everyone demanded an encore (and we got it!) They’re a band that you cannot help but love, and if you’ve not seen the documentary they recently put out- please go to YouTube and find it (it may still be there hopefully.) Not only will you too fall in love with the band and all they stand for, but you’ll just be in awe of their work ethic and how dedicated they are.

C.O.F.F.I.N are for everyone, and their live shows really make you feel it, and their live shows make you appreciate the band even more. I don’t know when they’ll be back in the UK but for now, I will hold onto this show as being one of the best things I’ve seen this year.

Thoughts of dread for the living. Pandering with the queen of sorrow. Pandering to the mirrors of no tomorrow.
Thoughts of dread for the living.
Pandering with the queen of sorrow.
Pandering to the mirrors of no tomorrow.

Depression can turn a trip to the corner shop into such a long negotiation with yourself that the place ends up closing long before you’ve picked up your keys. On “Feelings Are Monsters,” Berlin’s Night Nail give that dread seven eyes and seven legs. Brandon Robert counts them off as though taking inventory might make the damn thing easier to deal with.

Once upon a time, Robert was scraping by as a hired bassist in Hollywood, selling other people’s demos on the street, when a bandmate who put great stock in lucky numbers told him to “cheer up.” “It was degrading,” Robert says of those days. “But, we had to eat. Super dark times.”

“I decided that day to never play for someone else’s dream again,” Robert recalls. “I started recording my own music. I learned the hard way that no one tells your story for you. My bandmates actually did support me in my breakaway dream and ended up helping me tremendously with making my first singles and videos. But, I learned it’s really all on you to make it happen and rightfully so.”

That faith in lucky numbers has a sour afterlife in the refrain, where Robert sings, “Luck won’t change your number.” The track opens in a clatter, with bright flecks of guitar sticking out of the noise. Once the drums snap into time, the guitar winds through the sort of uneasy melody The Comsat Angels used to make sound inevitable, while the bassline lays down a gothic rock groove. A little over a minute in, Ruby Mai’s saxophone takes over from Robert’s low recitation. He comes back with his voice raised, then lets it sink in again, deeper, as he draws out his ode to the “queen of sorrow.” A rubbery bass break gives way to another round of counting before the guitar takes the song out.

Director Ilija Gavrilenko and editor Jean De Oliveira keep returning to the band under blue light, with black wisps spreading across the frame. Between those shots, a skull-faced figure in a wide black hat rides a lime-green scooter and lopes around a courtyard carpeted with fallen leaves. It looks like somebody sent a horror-movie ghoul out to run an errand.
Watch the video for “Feelings Are Monsters” below.

Night Nail formed in Los Angeles in 2013 and moved to Berlin before releasing their 2018 debut, LA Demons , on Cleopatra Records. March To Autumn followed on Cold Transmission in 2020, and Metropolis released Fates Explained in 2023. William Faith and Sven Wolff handled mixing and post-production on Night Nail’s fourth studio album, Infinite Fountain . Wolff worked on “Feelings Are Monsters” at Berlin’s Cosmonaut Studio, with Night Nail co-producing and Alex Lee contributing additional synths.

There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying their miserable bills while history quietly buries the evidence. Human civilization has developed an extraordinary talent for committing atrocities, commemorating the dead, and finding fresh excuses to repeat the process. Somewhere in this grand procession of moral bankruptcy, Seattle’s Profit Prison has found sufficient inspiration to write a disco song about the unbearable weight of collective guilt.

The solo project of Parker Lautensleger, whose musical history includes Anteinferno, Bhereg, Victims Panel, and Excarnated Entity, has spent nearly a decade exploring the more psychologically disturbed possibilities of electronic pop. His latest single, In Memoriam, taken from the forthcoming album Why art thou wroth? And why is thy countenance fallen? , sounds like Bronski Beat wandering into a particularly unpleasant historical reckoning, with electronic pioneer Gershon Kingsley conducting the proceedings from behind an enormous bank of synthesizers.

The arrangement possesses a strange, almost indecent sweetness. Synthesizers trace delicate melodic figures above a measured electronic rhythm, their crystalline repetitions creating the impression of a forgotten European dance record rescued from somebody’s flooded basement. Lautensleger sings with a trembling, distant resignation, his voice occupying the uncomfortable space between Neil Young’s wounded sincerity and the exquisite emotional distress of early synthpop by Das Kabinette, Depeche Mode, and others you might find on the Some Bizzare Compilation. Every syllable seems burdened by information its owner would dearly prefer to forget.

And what dreadful information it is. The lyrics describe a family whose apparently stable existence has been overturned by events unfolding near a border, where some unspecified act of violence has left questions that nobody seems willing to answer. Children inherit uncertainty, the dead receive their solemn acknowledgments, and the living are forced to contemplate the possibility that their own moral identities have been built upon carefully maintained ignorance. The song’s repeated interrogations grow increasingly desperate, suggesting a confrontation with somebody whose participation in an atrocity has become impossible to dismiss. Beneath the delicate electronic flourishes lies the hideous proposition that ordinary people can commit extraordinary acts of cruelty and subsequently spend entire lifetimes inventing explanations for themselves.

In Memoriam ‘s synthesizers maintain their patient, hypnotic progression while the words wander into the ugliest corners of human responsibility. You could conceivably dance to this record, which raises some rather uncomfortable questions about the emotional usefulness of disco. Lautensleger leaves those questions unanswered, however, allowing the music to continue its beautiful, merciless rotations while the accumulated weight of memory threatens to crush everything beneath it.

The video takes on a philosophical matter, as though we’re prisoners in Plato’s cave, watching distorted projections of events whose true nature remains somewhere beyond our comprehension. The road stretches onward, the lights assault our vision, and every image seems to conceal a fragment of some dreadful revelation.

The very British problem of GB Music Radio
GB News has launched an all-British radio station. As nationalistic thinkers so often do, they've oversimplified what it means to be British, and diluted the quality of their output in the…

How do you find common ground between a Guardian reader and a Daily Mail reader? Get them talking about British music. Somewhere down the line, they’ll share some musical common ground, or at least bond over their reverence – despite said reverence likely coming from different places – of the factory of musical greatness that is this strange little island.

For the right wing, perhaps it’s a beacon of what makes Great Britain greater than anywhere else. For the left, our music and culture might be the one thing about this country they can feel proud of in an era of decaying support structures and rampant division.

There’s something ironic, then, about right-wing slop spewers GB News positioning their new all-British radio station as a source of unity. Upon its announcement last month, Chief Revenue Officer Ross Sergeant said: “GB Music Radio gives advertisers something genuinely new: a station built around a single, warm idea that almost everyone in this country can get behind.”

Music should be the great unifier. Can a radio station really do that, though, when it’s had red, white and blue vomited all over it courtesy of arguably the most polarising, untrustworthy and hateful news brand in the country? It’s doubtful. For that reason alone, plenty of people wouldn’t touch it with a bargepole.

In fact, something about its announcement felt ridiculous enough to be satirical, especially with how it positioned its show names, like ‘Great British Drive Home’ and ‘Great British Breakfast’. So this is a station for people who chant ‘Come on Ingerland’ as they wolf down their bacon sarnies in the morning before sitting in their very Bri’ish traffic jam (in a vehicle that is decidedly not British)?

Sergeant added: “British music is a shared passion that cuts across generations, and we look forward to helping brands become part of the soundtrack to our listeners' day, from Breakfast with Paul [Coyte] to weekend mornings with Nana [Akua].” Coyte and Akua are already established names on GB News, the former presenting sports shows before pivoting back to music, while Akua recently went viral for a heated exchange with a guest on a panel last month.

Consequently, 'All British, all day’ once again spits in the face of any sort of unity. There’s no hiding the nationalism behind it, as it turns music into a cultural battleground it has dominance over, wresting it out of progressive hands into something it can call its own.

The arts and culture sectors, particularly music, are overwhelmingly left-wing , and music has for decades been a site of community building and changemaking, from Seventies punk values to recent calls for boycotts and solidarity with Palestine.
More recently, when the right have wanted a piece of this, they’ve even turned to AI-generated figureheads such as Danny Bones, who we investigated on the podcast.

GB Music Radio’s other problem is it tries to make the idea of Britishness far more simple and far less nuanced than it is in reality. Who gets to be considered British? What about mixed-nationality artists? Does AI count?

A spokesperson tells Drowned in Sound: “We celebrate British music in the broadest possible sense. British artists, or groups who are British or have British members. For example we will feature Fleetwood Mac. GB Music already features AI generated content in our hourly traffic AI reports but there are no plans for any fully AI songs."

It’s better that it’s broad, of course. To strip away all but the most ‘purely’ British artists certainly leaves the pool looking about as bland and beige as a plate of potato smileys sans sauce. Looking at what they've played at the time of writing, the playlist includes Lewis Capaldi's 'Survive', Pulp's 'Disco 2000' Kajagoogoo's 'Too Shy', Rainbow's 'Since You've Been Gone', David Bowie and Queen's 'Under Pressure' and Duffy's 'Mercy.' These are all songs you could hear if you whacked on Heart, Virgin Radio and the like. It's not all that different from a lot of middle-of-the-road mainstream radio, except without the variety an all-nationality playlist could offer.

12 Common Holiday-Party Disasters—And How to Fix Them ASAP
From kitchen mishaps to awkward moments with guests, even the most carefully planned celebration can go awry. Here's how to keep your cool and save the day.

I entertain a lot around the holidays, and I mean a lot: an annual party with former work colleagues; a Hanukkah dinner (I’m not Jewish, but my crew love latkes); a homemade-pizza night and gingerbread-house-building session with my niece, her BFF and their moms; and, of course, the Feast of the Seven Fishes, the Italian American Christmas Eve tradition .

I’m a planner, and an incredibly organized one, at that. I’ve got spreadsheets with shopping lists, ingredient lists, detailed to-do lists … you get the picture. And yet, no matter how prepared I am, things happen. Like the time I dropped a baking dish of perfectly browned, crispy-edged roasted potatoes on my tile floor, or the time—or, should I say, times?—I ran out of ice. Because here’s the thing: Holiday-party disasters are inevitable. You can plan for every possible scenario, but eventually something will go sideways. And when it does, well, the party must go on.

The trick is knowing how to recover without turning a minor snafu into a major production. As event planner Renee Patrone Rhinehart puts it, “Your guests probably have no idea something went wrong until you start announcing it to everyone.” Her advice? “Just roll with it!”

To find out how to roll with a dozen of the most common holiday-party disasters when you’re hosting , I went to the experts. Iron Chef Alex Guarnaschelli and renowned Southern chef Carla Hall weigh in on turkey troubles and other food emergencies; event planners Rhinehart and Marcy Blum share their secrets for keeping a party on track; etiquette expert Myka Meier offers advice for navigating awkward social situations; and licensed marriage and family therapist Nari Jeter, PhD, weighs in on emotionally charged moments.

So whether your turkey is taking forever to cook, an unexpected guest arrives or your uncle decides today is the perfect time to reignite that family feud, here’s how to save the celebration—and your sanity. Party on!

You’re still getting dressed, the kitchen is a disaster zone, and the appetizers aren’t even out yet. Then the doorbell rings—20 minutes before you expected anyone. Now you need to switch into host mode, and fast.

What to do: Welcome them warmly, offer a drink , and, if you’re comfortable, give them a small task, like putting on the music or lighting candles. “You’re early! Perfect timing. Why it works: You don’t need to drop everything to entertain an early arrival. A little hospitality goes a long way, and giving someone a simple job can make them feel included rather than in the way. It can even turn into a bonding moment with your new guest!

You planned dinner for eight, set the table for eight and made just enough food for eight. Then someone shows up with an unexpected plus-one. You could panic about the extra chair and plate, or you could get creative and make it work.

What to do: Take a breath , pull up an extra chair and welcome that person as though you expected them all along. “As a host, your goal is to make everyone feel welcome, even when you’re caught off guard,” says Meier. Simply say, “How lovely to meet you! Come on in.” After all, she adds, “It was not the guest’s fault they were asked to be there, and you don’t want them to feel that when arriving.”

Blum says to have card stock and a pen on hand to make an extra place card, if necessary. Rhinehart recommends stretching the meal with whatever you have—bread, salad or an extra side—and resisting the urge to announce that you weren’t prepared for another person.

Why it works: You’re taking charge, being an excellent hostess and rolling with the surprise. Making a fuss, on the other hand, can turn a small logistical hiccup into an awkward moment. As Rhinehart says, “Nobody needs to know!”

How do you document family history when there are so many missing pieces? By tackling it little by little, says Allison Singleton, the genealogy services manager at the Genealogy Center. “There will be gaps of information you don’t know,” she says. But don’t let that stop you.

That being said, you’ll have a lot more luck if you have a method to the madness. That’s why I reached out to a few experts who do this for a living and could lay it out in simple terms for us. How on earth do you even start this kind of project?
Before you dive into documenting your family’s history, determine your goal. “Knowing where you want to end up tells you where to start and how much you need to gather,” Shoa says.

Next, collect supplies. Shoa says you’ll need several plastic bins, colorful index cards for categorizing batches of photos, an archival pencil, a 2TB or 4TB external hard drive for storage, nitrile gloves for handling photos, and a notebook or spreadsheet for tracking.

Then, gather the documentation you already have and group it into categories. Think of this like taking an inventory. “Put like with like,” Shoa says. “The albums, the slides, the negatives and the VHS tapes should each have their own piles.” In addition to photos and videos, include things like old letters , newspaper clippings, obituaries, birth and death certificates, and recipe cards. “These items are full of clues about your family history,” Singleton notes. After you’ve grouped everything, you’ll dig into each category. (More on that below.)

Keep in mind that you don’t need to do everything at once. “Start small—with one photograph, one document, one family story, one person or one question—and see how your research progresses,” Singleton advises. After all, you don’t want to get overwhelmed before you even really start!
